slides.title: Role Playing
content: Role Playing

Students act out the role of a character in a scenario to prepare for situations they may encounter while fulfilling their duties

Can be used when training personnel for variety of tasks or situations

slides.title: Role Playing
content: Role Playing

At end of role play, instructor debriefs participants and observers about objective of activity — Debriefing gives students opportunity to explain their feelings and actions during role playing activity

Some role playing scenarios may be emotionally charged — Instructor should allow time for students to successfully separate themselves from role they played

Instructor should summarize scenario and reinforce any positive behavior exhibited

slides.title: Role Playing: Advantages
content: Role Playing: Advantages

Encourages application of knowledge and safe practice of skills

Permits students to practice under conditions that simulate an incident without danger of fatal consequences

slides.title: Role Playing: Advantages
content: Role Playing: Advantages

Improves understanding of critical features of interpersonal relations

Allows students to identify multiple approaches to a problem

slides.title: Role Playing: Advantages
content: Role Playing: Advantages

Increases development of empathy as students discuss their own perspectives and listen to their classmates’ opinions

Helps develop critical awareness

Prepares students for emotionally challenging events, such as dealing with trauma patients

slides.title: Role Playing: Disadvantages
content: Role Playing: Disadvantages

Preparation can be complicated and time-consuming

Can take time to perform and may result in students digressing from the topic when bored, uninterested, or see no value in the activity

Requires students to identify, at least superficially, with the characters and scenario

slides.title: NOTE
content: NOTE

When debriefing a role-playing scenario, instructors should remind students that actions taken during the scenario should not be considered part of a fellow student’s personal character, but rather part of a larger training situation designed to ingrain situational behavior and skills.

slides.title: Simulations
content: Simulations

Training simulations allow students to participate in scenarios that represent situations they are likely to encounter on the job

May take many forms, from practical training evolutions using demonstration devices to technology-centered activities such as computer-based training (CBT)

Permit students to experience a situation, make decisions, and see the results of their decisions without negative consequences

slides.title: Simulations
content: Simulations

Key to all simulations is to ensure they effectively reflect equipment, procedures, protocols, and situations students will encounter on duty

May be tailored to type and scope of the training—most simulations include role-playing elements

Examples
Tabletop emergency management drill
Confined-space rescue training
Computer-based training

slides.title: Field and Laboratory Experiences
content: Field and Laboratory Experiences

Field and laboratory experiences provide students with demonstrations and simulations, allowing students to inspect, use, test, and evaluate equipment or processes

Prior to learning in a laboratory or field environment, students should learn safe, applicable procedures to ensue safe learning environment

slides.title: Field and Laboratory Experiences
content: Field and Laboratory Experiences

In the field, students are typically given a tour of an installation; they may be permitted to observe a fire detection and suppression systems test or see steps required to replace a component

Field experiences tend to be less controlled than laboratory settings, so students may not be able to handle components; on the other hand, they will be able to see systems functioning on larger scale than is often possible in a laboratory

slides.title: Field and Laboratory Experiences
content: Field and Laboratory Experiences

In a laboratory, students can see models of equipment, such as cutaways of apparatus engines, pumps, or sprinkler control valves

They may perform chemistry experiments to simulate fire behavior or fire spread in an enclosed space

In the controlled environment of a laboratory, the instructor explains the equipment or process, demonstrates steps required, observes students as they repeat the skills

slides.title: Field and Laboratory Experiences
content: Field and Laboratory Experiences

Students may work independently or in groups

Instructors may choose to give students a challenge, such as providing them with a defective SCBA regulator and asking them to repair it

slides.title: Learning Objective 5
content: Learning Objective 5
Describe competency-based learning in the fire and emergency services.

slides.title: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services
content: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services

In the fire and emergency services:

Students should be competent with one set of requisite information and skills before they progress to a new one

Competency-based learning (CBL), sometimes referred to as mastery learning, requires each student successfully master the learning objectives or outcomes of the lesson or course

slides.title: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services
content: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services

In the competency-based learning approach, instructors are provided with the specific criteria (standards) that students must meet during testing for competency
 
Information is stated in the learning objectives

slides.title: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services
content: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services

Focuses on competency
Meets individual needs
Provides immediate, specific feedback
Employs modules and multimedia
Depends on instructors
Meets specific objectives
Uses criterion-referenced testing

slides.title: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services
content: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services

The competency approach uses criterion-referenced teaching, learning, and assessments; and focuses attention on learning objectives

Students who have problems meeting the desired criteria on their initial efforts get additional instruction, time, and opportunities to perform to the acceptable level

slides.title: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services
content: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services

Learning objectives are written to establish the criteria for competency

Identify and clearly describe the learning outcome (behavior)

Define the important conditions under which the students will perform (conditions)

Define the criterion of acceptable performance (degree)

slides.title: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services
content: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services

When the material is difficult or complex, instructors may need to schedule additional instruction time so that students can assimilate complex concepts

No student should proceed to new material until he or she has become competent in the basic requisite material

slides.title: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services: Advantages
content: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services: Advantages

Students are prepared to advance to more complex knowledge or skills

Prior knowledge is used as a building block for new skills, which can make gaining competency easier for the student

slides.title: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services: Advantages
content: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services: Advantages

Students are made aware of the learning objectives from the beginning so that criteria for passing the course are never in question

Time is given to tailor learning to the student’s individual learner characteristics and learning style, which assists the student in gaining competency

slides.title: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services: Disadvantages
content: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services: Disadvantages

Instructors must plan for and provide extra time to ensure that all students become competent on the subject

More effort is required on the instructor’s part to determine students’ learning pace and to match it

slides.title: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services: Disadvantages
content: Competency-Based Learning in the Fire and Emergency Services: Disadvantages

Faster students may feel that slower classmates are holding them back

A wide variety of training materials must be available to meet the learning needs of all students

slides.title: Learning Objective 6
content: Learning Objective 6
Identify teaching strategies that 	encourage active learning.

slides.title: Teaching Strategies
content: Teaching Strategies

As instructors learn more about educating people, they often come to the realization that people learn differently depending on the topic

With these variations in mind, instructors can use different teaching strategies to adapt to changing learning environment and challenges

slides.title: Traditional Instructor-Led Training (ILT)
content: Traditional Instructor-Led Training (ILT)

Instructor-led training (ILT) is the most prevalent approach to teaching in the fire and emergency services

ILT has the advantage of being
Flexible
Economical
Familiar to both students and instructors

slides.title: Multiple Instructors
content: Multiple Instructors

Instructor-led learning environments traditionally have only one instructor serving in multiple roles; a variation is to split some of the responsibilities among multiple instructors or team teach.

In addition to sharing the workload, multiple instructors combine their knowledge and experience so students are better able to meet course learning objectives or outcomes; can be an effective educational technique and a unifying force between organizations

slides.title: Multiple Instructors
content: Multiple Instructors

In one variation, known as team teaching, multiple instructors teach the same topics at the same time with different groups of students

Team teaching provides a more effective use of class time and has smaller student-to-instructor ratios

slides.title: Multiple Instructors
content: Multiple Instructors

The instructor with the most knowledge or experience in a particular topic usually teaches the cognitive and demonstration portions of the lesson to all classes

That instructor then joins with other instructors in supervising the practical training evolution

slides.title: Multiple Instructors
content: Multiple Instructors

Provide an effective use of resources from multiple areas and specialties

Allow an instructional delivery method that works well when topic is broad

Provide students with an exposure to wide variety of teaching methods and skills training

Keep the attention of group by utilizing each instructor’s different voice, pace, and personality

slides.title: Multiple Instructors: Considerations
content: Multiple Instructors: Considerations

Make an extensive course plan that outlines each instructor’s role and time commitment

Maintain communication between all instructors to ensure course continuity and consistency

Choose instructors whose teaching styles contrast, yet balance one another

slides.title: Multiple Instructors
content: Multiple Instructors

Decide in advance who will teach which topic

Review all lesson outlines together so that each instructor knows what the others are doing

Agree on and use the same format for all instructional technology tools

Designate one lead instructor per topic

slides.title: Multiple Instructors
content: Multiple Instructors

Determine time commitments and require each instructor to adhere to them

Agree that all instructors will be present for the entire course, not just when it is their turn to teach

Meet with other instructors to review session results

slides.title: Generating and Maintaining Student Interest
content: Generating and Maintaining Student Interest

Instructor-led training relies on students’ interest for the overall class session to be successful

Interested students are open and responsive and want to concentrate on what they are learning, also more willing to actively participate in the learning process

To help maintain interest, instructors need to show students how they have a personal connection with the lesson

slides.title: Generating and Maintaining Student Interest: Strategies
content: Generating and Maintaining Student Interest: Strategies

slides.title: Generating and Maintaining Student Interest: Strategies
content: Generating and Maintaining Student Interest: Strategies

slides.title: Reinforcing Learning: Repetition and Behavioral Reinforcement
content: Reinforcing Learning: Repetition and Behavioral Reinforcement

Repetition involves repeating, re-emphasizing, and reviewing key points with the students

Behavioral reinforcement encourages students’ attempts to learn by acknowledging their successes and correcting their mistakes

slides.title: Reinforcing Learning
content: Reinforcing Learning

Intentional repetition is an important part of organizing a presentation

Through emphasis and repetition, instructors help students to recognize the importance of key points

Instructors should provide opportunities for students to apply knowledge and practice important skills in a safe learning environment

slides.title: Reinforcing Learning
content: Reinforcing Learning

Behavioral reinforcement is based on psychological theory that connects a change in behavior with consequences of that change

Behavioral reinforcement establishes rewards (positive reinforcement) for students’ successes or good behavior and negative consequences for their failures or bad behavior

slides.title: Reinforcing Learning
content: Reinforcing Learning

In the fire and emergency services, rewards for success include promotion or commendations

In the learning environment, positive reinforcement may be as simple as instructor’s compliment or encouragement after student properly performs skill or masters theoretical concept

Educational research has demonstrated students learn faster, make permanent behavioral changes when their successes are met with meaningful positive reinforcement

slides.title: Blended or Hybrid Learning
content: Blended or Hybrid Learning

Blended or hybrid learning combines traditional (face-to-face) and online teaching methods

Instructors who use the hybrid learning environment need to be very organized, disciplined to maintain high level of student satisfaction and performance

With the reduction of a formal structure, it is easy for both the instructor and student to become frustrated and/or confused about what is happening and what needs to happen in the course

slides.title: Student-Centered Learning
content: Student-Centered Learning

Instructor shifts the focus to the students

Instructor provides students with active learning activities and becomes more of a facilitator than a traditional teacher

This method of instruction, more than the traditional method, leads to an increased depth of knowledge and understanding of the material

slides.title: Flipping the Classroom
content: Flipping the Classroom

In the traditional classroom model, the instructor lectures over new material in class, and the student is assigned exercises, activities to complete at home

If students have questions or difficulties with the homework, they have to wait until the next class period to ask the instructor for help

The flipped classroom reverses that traditional teaching model

slides.title: Flipping the Classroom
content: Flipping the Classroom

Instead of students coming to class for a lecture, they read and study the new material at home

When they come to class, students have more time to ask questions, discuss the material, and engage in activities that reinforce their learning

By bringing active learning activities into the classroom, the instructor can reduce student frustration and provide a more positive learning environment

slides.title: Computer Simulation
content: Computer Simulation

Many training programs use instructional technology tools such as CBT modules and programs that allow students to work at their own pace

CBT may also be used in a more structured format to provide distance learning

slides.title: Computer Simulation
content: Computer Simulation

CBT programs minimize interaction between a student and an instructor

Instructors may present an illustrated lecture remotely over the Internet or closed-circuit television or may only be involved in answering questions that arise as students read information on their own and complete assignments

AHJ should inform instructor of products, instructional technology tools he or she will be using to deliver instruction

slides.title: Computer Simulation
content: Computer Simulation

CBT platforms require software to function effectively, and each may have unique requirements

Instructors must make sure that students’ computers have necessary

Internet access
Sufficient speed
Enough internal memory

slides.title: Computer Simulation
content: Computer Simulation

Instructors must make sure that students’ computers have necessary

Internet browsers
Computer operating systems (for example, Windows™ or Macintosh™)
Word processing programs
Document readers, such as Adobe Acrobat Reader®
Unique software needed for the course

slides.title: Computer Simulation
content: Computer Simulation

When facilitating CBT, instructors sometimes take on the role of computer support specialist

Instructors may be able to answer some questions; however, if they cannot promptly resolve a student’s technical problems, instructors should contact someone else who can do so

No student should be penalized because a piece of equipment, software application, or computer does not work properly

slides.title: CAUTION
content: CAUTION
After an email or electronic file has been deleted, traces still remain on the user’s computer system.

slides.title: Computer Simulation
content: Computer Simulation

Instructors should familiarize themselves with all the software used in the CBT system

Many of these tools are useful for any distance learning scenario, and instructors may wish to augment a distance learning program by using these tools

slides.title: Computer Simulation: Software Use
content: Computer Simulation: Software Use

Wikis, blogs, and file sharing services
Social networking systems
Live streaming audio and video
Chat sessions
Teleconferencing and web conferencing
Course management system (CMS)
Learning management system (LMS)

slides.title: Computer Simulation
content: Computer Simulation

Instructors using CBT should be aware of the ways that this format may interfere with their ability to effectively deliver a message

Feedback from students is minimal, and the technology presents an additional barrier between the instructor and the students

slides.title: Computer Simulation: Adjustments
content: Computer Simulation: Adjustments

slides.title: Computer Simulation: Adjustments
content: Computer Simulation: Adjustments

slides.title: Self-Directed Learning
content: Self-Directed Learning

In self-directed learning or independent learning:
Individual students work at their own pace to accomplish course objectives, including the completion of tasks and skills in a predetermined format and the completion of work within a defined timeframe

Students are solely responsible for achieving these objectives{
Which may be determined by the instructor or chosen by the student

slides.title: Self-Directed Learning
content: Self-Directed Learning

Instructor is not involved in the delivery of the training, but may act as a facilitator and monitor to ensure students complete work correctly

Effectiveness of this distance learning method is heavily dependent on the student’s level of motivation

Instructor and student schedule several meetings to monitor progress of the independent study

slides.title: Self-Directed Learning
content: Self-Directed Learning

Instructors are available to answer questions, evaluate learning achievements, and guide the student, but the learning process is completely the student’s responsibility

Self-directed learning often motivates students to discover information and resources beyond lesson requirements

Not all types of training programs, particularly basic-level skill programs, are suited to this type of instruction

slides.title: Individualized Instruction
content: Individualized Instruction

Another variation on instructor-led training, individualized instruction, has instructors adapt and/or adjust their teaching methods to address the needs of each student in the class and focus on his or her specific learner characteristics and learning styles

Instructor manages learning resources, guides students, and interacts with them but is not the sole or primary resource for learning as in the traditional instructor-led classroom

slides.title: Individualized Instruction
content: Individualized Instruction

Individualized instruction may also utilize some features of a self-directed learning plan and CBT

This approach may enable students who would not succeed in a typical learning environment to successfully achieve learning objectives

slides.title: Individualized Instruction: Basis
content: Individualized Instruction: Basis

A student’s needs and learner characteristics

Learning objectives or competencies required by the occupation

Instructional strategies and media that meet the needs of the student

slides.title: Individualized Instruction
content: Individualized Instruction

During individualized instruction, the instructor meets frequently with a student to

Evaluate progress

Prescribe new learning objectives or different learning methods

Provide encouragement

slides.title: Individualized Instruction
content: Individualized Instruction

Many organizations use individualized instruction techniques in their training programs, including

Learning activity packets
Tutorial instruction
Programmed learning

slides.title: Certification Testing: Process 1
content: Certification Testing: Process 1

Instructor Directions : Process 1 Final Presentation Directions
General Information:
This criterion referenced process-based assessment was developed to test the job performance requirements in NFPA 1041 Fire and Emergency Services Instructor I 2019 Edition. 
This testing was developed using the process-based assessment methodology.

slides.title: Certification Testing: Process 1
content: Certification Testing: Process 1

Process #1 is used to perform certification testing for the following JPRs: 
4.2.2 Assemble course materials
4.3.2 Review instructional materials
4.3.3 Adapt a lesson plan
4.4.2 Organize the learning environment
4.4.3 Present and adjust prepared lessons
4.4.4 Adjust to differences in learner characteristics
4.4.5 Operate instructional technology tools and demonstration devices

slides.title: Certification Testing: Process 1
content: Certification Testing: Process 1

Reference: Chapter 4 Skill Sheet 4-1 Page 85
Reference: Chapter 5 Skill Sheet 5-1 Page 103
Reference: Chapter 6 Skill Sheet 6-1 Page 137
Process #1 is a final course comprehensive presentation and is graded individually. 
Each candidate will be assigned one prepared lesson plan and will receive a blank copy of the Fire Instructor I Process Assessment Rubric. 
The testing packet with the lesson plan and materials are assigned two days prior to testing.

slides.title: Certification Testing: Process 1
content: Certification Testing: Process 1

The candidate has the allotted time of two days of both classroom and outside classroom time to”
 assemble the materials and equipment listed, 
review and prepare, practice, adapt as needed to the audience stated, 
organize the classroom or environment listed, 
adjust to any changes given and 
become familiar with and operated the instructional media or other instructional tool assigned or offered to the candidate. 

***The course instructor is responsible for providing the instructional tools and ensuring that candidates are familiar with the equipment prior to testing.

slides.title: Certification Testing: Process 1
content: Certification Testing: Process 1

The assigned prepared lesson plan time frame is 15 minutes but with a range of 13-17 minutes in which to present the material.
 Questions from the audience will not add or take away from the required time for the presentation but are encouraged. 
Some of the topics in the assigned lesson plans may be repeated. 
Candidates are graded on presentation preparation and techniques only and not on the content of the lesson plan.   


The assigned lesson plans were taken from the IFSTA Essentials of Firefighting textbook and are designed to teach basic firefighting in a recruit school setting.

slides.title: Certification Testing: Process 1
content: Certification Testing: Process 1

Testing Scenario: The audience members in the Process #1 testing scenario are firefighter recruit candidates that have scored poorly on weekly quizzes and are attending a small group review. 
The candidate must assess this audience and make the necessary adjustments. The candidates are told that the firefighter recruits have a variety of preferred learning styles. 
The classroom environment should be adjusted for the number of student participants. 
They are told a classroom in the training center has been reserved for the review. 
The classroom provided for the candidates must be safe and conducive to learning but the candidate may adjust chairs, tables, etc. as needed.

slides.title: Certification Testing: Process 1
content: Certification Testing: Process 1

The candidate will present the final presentation to an audience of no less than five Fire Instructor I classmates, firefighter recruits, coworkers, or other available prospective students who would role play as fire recruits. This scenario may be adjusted for EMS or other emergency personnel if needed.  
Each candidate will be evaluated by at least two evaluators who have not been involved in the teaching of the course. Each evaluator will grade using a separate grading rubric for each candidate. The grading rubrics will be returned to the Certification Office at the end of the testing session.

slides.title: Certification Testing: Process 1
content: Certification Testing: Process 1

A list of equipment such as turnout gear, fire extinguishers, etc. has been provided on the lesson plan but the candidate is required to utilize at least two pieces of equipment from the list. 
The student may assemble additional equipment as needed but must assemble at least two from the equipment listed.  
Each lesson plan contains at least three prepared Powerpoint slides. 
The candidate may add more as needed but must use the minimum three slides. 
The candidate may edit the provided slides. The candidate should have access to the audio/visual equipment two days prior to practice and gain familiarity. Again, course instructors should ensure that each candidate is familiar with the equipment.

slides.title: Certification Testing: Process 1
content: Certification Testing: Process 1

Evaluator. All evaluators for the process-based assessments should be trained prior to evaluating at a testing event for Fire Instructor I. 
Each evaluator will be given a copy of the prepared lesson plans along with a copy if the Fire Instructor I Process Assessment Rubric for each candidate. 
The rubric is used to document the behaviors and processes of the candidate being tested that are observed by the evaluator for each JPR.

slides.title: Learning Objective 1
content: Learning Objective 1
Describe ways instructors can address individual student needs in fire and emergency services training.

slides.title: Individual Student Needs
content: Individual Student Needs

Some students will be quick to grasp a concept or learn a skill, while others may need additional resources to remain current with the class schedule

Independent of learner characteristics or learning style, some students show behaviors and learning backgrounds that require more attention

Instructors should learn to recognize the behaviors of individuals who will need additional assistance, ideally before a class session is disrupted

slides.title: Individual Student Needs
content: Individual Student Needs

Instructors may encounter students with various learning backgrounds and learning abilities, including

Diverse background/history
Low literacy levels
Learning disabilities
Students requiring adaptations
High learning abilities

slides.title: Diversity
content: Diversity

Over time, research has shown the value in increasing diversity in many environments

Each unique perspective may challenge the assumptions of the others and strengthen best practices

Instructors must be careful to promote a welcoming environment for all students

slides.title: Diversity: Basis
content: Diversity: Basis

slides.title: Diversity
content: Diversity

Instructors must be careful to promote a welcoming environment for all students

In contrast to the positive benefits of diversity, differences between people of different cultural backgrounds may disrupt communication

slides.title: Diversity: Cultural and Background Differences May Stem From Variables
content: Diversity: Cultural and Background Differences May Stem From Variables

slides.title: Diversity: Variables
content: Diversity: Variables

In addition to cultural differences, a class member who is not a native speaker of the primary language used in the classroom may have more difficulty parsing or relating the terms used throughout the class

These complications are compounded as multiple backgrounds and languages are presented in the same classroom

slides.title: Low Literacy Levels
content: Low Literacy Levels

Literacy, the ability to read, write, and generally function in a given language, is a critical skill in most workplaces

To some degree, skills may be taught during hands-on classes, but most classwork assignments and many evaluations will have a written component

slides.title: Low Literacy Levels
content: Low Literacy Levels

The U.S. Workforce Investment Act of 1998 indicates that adults should reach an 8th-grade reading level before entering the workforce

Students who do not meet that benchmark, whether because they are not native speakers of a language or some other reason, may have difficulty taking notes and keeping up with the material as presented

slides.title: Low Literacy Levels
content: Low Literacy Levels

Should the gap in a student’s literacy level be significant, an instructor may help the student research and access any available assistance

If students demonstrate low literacy levels, they may be self-conscious about gaps in knowledge and/or abilities

Instructors must be careful not to imply that illiteracy is a factor of the student’s intelligence and instead work with the student to find resources that will help the student succeed

slides.title: Low Literacy Levels
content: Low Literacy Levels

Some students may complete twelve years of schooling while functionally illiterate, and they may not know they have a gap in knowledge

It may be sufficient for an instructor to make simple modifications to resources

slides.title: Low Literacy Levels: Locally Produced Documents Features
content: Low Literacy Levels: Locally Produced Documents Features

slides.title: Low Literacy Levels: Locally Produced Documents Features
content: Low Literacy Levels: Locally Produced Documents Features

slides.title: Special Needs
content: Special Needs

Students with any kind of special need are at a disadvantage when compared with students without a special need

Instructors will usually be able to identify students who are struggling with the requirements of a class soon after beginning

slides.title: Special Needs
content: Special Needs

Instructors should communicate at the beginning of a course or lesson that anyone seeking reasonable accommodations should contact them privately

The private meeting will allow the instructor to identify appropriate accommodations

This availability for consultation, and indication of the possibility for accommodations should also be included in the course syllabus

slides.title: Special Needs
content: Special Needs

Students with limited learning disabilities may be able to perform class requirements at or above the level of their cohort with some accommodations in specific areas

Students with specific learning disabilities may not be able to perform at the rate of their classmates in certain subjects or tasks

These students will be able to learn and perform at the same level but at a slower pace

slides.title: Special Needs
content: Special Needs

Learning disabilities are not an indicator of intelligence or motivation; they are a wide variety of neurological-based processing difficulties

As learning disabilities are increasingly researched and managed, more people who experience difficulties in a learning environment are evaluated

Adults with a learning disability may not know why they have trouble learning, in part because available evaluations were not available when they were children

slides.title: Special Needs
content: Special Needs

slides.title: Special Needs
content: Special Needs

Students may have average to high intelligence but perform poorly on tests due to their specific learning disability

In legal liability context, students seeking accommodations are required by federal law to show specific learning disability documentation

To acquire documentation, students need to be diagnosed by an appropriate professional

slides.title: Special Needs
content: Special Needs

An organization’s human resources department may be able to provide testing and referral assistance

Government agencies and large private organizations that provide training may offer evaluation and assistance for employees with learning disabilities or refer them to appropriate agencies

Some accommodations may require documentation such as a written diagnosis

slides.title: Special Needs: Accommodations Available at Discretion of the Instructor
content: Special Needs: Accommodations Available at Discretion of the Instructor

slides.title: Special Needs: Accommodations Available at Discretion of the Instructor
content: Special Needs: Accommodations Available at Discretion of the Instructor

slides.title: Special Needs: Three U.S. Discrimination Protection Laws
content: Special Needs: Three U.S. Discrimination Protection Laws

slides.title: Special Needs
content: Special Needs
When an instructor knows that a student with a specific learning disability will be in his or her class, the instructor should focus on that condition

slides.title: Special Needs: Accommodations for Struggling Students
content: Special Needs: Accommodations for Struggling Students

slides.title: Special Needs
content: Special Needs

An instructor may also reevaluate and revise the subject matter or instructional methods

A student may have difficulty grasping information and skills in one lesson or category yet may excel in other areas 

Instructors should develop assignments and lesson plans that can be tailored to individual learning styles and student needs

slides.title: Special Needs
content: Special Needs

Some students can become conscious of their difficulties as other students work faster with fewer mistakes

Instructors must be careful to encourage all students to treat each other equally

Instructors should always provide positive feedback as students accomplish course objectives

slides.title: High Learning Abilities
content: High Learning Abilities

Some students appear to learn without trying
Will usually accomplish more than is expected of average students
May study, learn well without much supervision
When students perceive they can understand and retain material more quickly:
May lose motivation
Become disengaged from the learning process
Become disruptive, unsafe to other students
May leave the course with a low opinion of the instructor, curriculum, or the training department

slides.title: High Learning Abilities: Instructor Approaches
content: High Learning Abilities: Instructor Approaches

Instructors can turn the presence of high ability learners into an asset
These students can be given more creative assignments and asked to present their findings to the class

slides.title: High Learning Abilities: Instructor Approaches
content: High Learning Abilities: Instructor Approaches

Another approach for instructors is to task a high ability learner
Be a tutor or note taker for another student
While assisting other individuals, adult high ability learners improve their own retention

At the same time, the student receiving the help may feel more comfortable learning from a peer rather than an instructor

slides.title: High Learning Abilities: Instructor Approaches
content: High Learning Abilities: Instructor Approaches

Students with high learning abilities need to be engaged with assignments that meet their ability level:
Even if these assignments are beyond the scope of what the rest of the class is doing

slides.title: Learning Objective 2
content: Learning Objective 2
Describe students’ rights in an 	educational setting.

slides.title: Students’ Rights: In An Educational Setting
content: Students’ Rights: In An Educational Setting

Privacy of records and test scores

Freedom to hold and express an opinion different from that of the instructor or organization

Equal access to the learning environment

slides.title: Students’ Rights: In An Educational Setting
content: Students’ Rights: In An Educational Setting

Fair and equal treatment in class

A learning environment free of discrimination or harassment

A safe learning environment

slides.title: Students’ Rights
content: Students’ Rights

Any rules or regulations that may be perceived as infringing on students’ substantive rights should be reviewed, validated, and communicated to students at the beginning of instruction; these must be consistently applied throughout the program

In some cases, it is necessary to protect the physical safety of students during the learning process; a reasonable regulation may be seen as an infringement of student rights

slides.title: Learning Objective 3
content: Learning Objective 3
Discuss techniques instructors use to manage student behavior.

slides.title: Student Behavior Management
content: Student Behavior Management

Instructors must be able to prevent disruptive students from interfering with the class, or they risk losing the other students’ respect and failing to accomplish the learning objectives

The ultimate goal of student behavior management is the steady, safe participation by all students in a learning environment

slides.title: Student Behavior Management
content: Student Behavior Management

With adults, peer pressure can be effective to manage behavior, but it is ultimately the instructor’s responsibility to deal with disruptive students

Even when peer pressure is partially effective, an instructor may speak to disruptive students in private or take stronger disciplinary measures

Most organizations have policies for managing issues involving student problems and performance; however, the best action is to prevent problems before they occur

slides.title: Reviewing Policies
content: Reviewing Policies

One of the first priorities for an instructor is to review the rules, regulations, and policies of the training division with students

Promotes, supports, and enforces these policies so that students follow and respect them

slides.title: NOTE
content: NOTE
The instructor should brief students on the rules of the facility early in the course or class.

slides.title: Counseling
content: Counseling
Some students engage in disruptive behavior when they have difficulty meeting learning objectives or adjusting to training; such students may benefit from counseling

slides.title: Counseling Actions
content: Counseling Actions

slides.title: Counseling
content: Counseling

Counseling sessions between instructors and students should focus on issues relevant to the students’ progress in class

Unqualified instructors should never assume the role of therapist

Instructor should follow organizational procedures

Students can typically access counseling through EAP

slides.title: CAUTION
content: CAUTION
Instructors and staff members should seek additional help if a student’s concerns appear to be more complicated than they can address in their formal capacity or level of training.

slides.title: Counseling
content: Counseling

Counseling sessions between students and instructors must take place in a private and controllable area

The instructor should be careful to emphasize that the counseling session is intended to resolve problems, not to force any specific resolution

Students may not willingly offer information about troublesome situations; instructors must encourage students to express and explain their feelings

slides.title: Counseling
content: Counseling

The sense of partnership created during successful counseling makes students more likely to listen to the instructor’s advice

Instructors must learn and practice appropriate counseling and positive reinforcement methods that motivate students to perform properly

slides.title: Counseling
content: Counseling

Training organizations usually have a formal process for documenting behavioral issues
Typically involves completing some type of counseling form

New instructors must be aware of the organization’s process and need to realize that it is more than the simple, immediate measures they can implement in class

Some organizations may be required to maintain records on counseling for accreditation purposes

slides.title: Counseling: General Guidelines
content: Counseling: General Guidelines

Meet and talk with the student

Use facts to precisely describe the individual’s behavior

State student expectations and record them on the counseling form

slides.title: Counseling: General Guidelines
content: Counseling: General Guidelines

Discuss the issue and possible solutions with the student

Explain what actions will be taken if the student does not comply with the objectives and solutions

slides.title: Counseling: General Guidelines
content: Counseling: General Guidelines

slides.title: Counseling
content: Counseling

If counseling fails, instructors must take steps to alleviate the situation
Further conversations may help the situation
Instructor must again conduct a meeting 
Privately, calmly, focus on constructive steps that can be taken

Demonstrating a sincere interest in students is more effective than making them feel inferior or inadequate

slides.title: Coaching
content: Coaching

Disruptive behavior often results from frustration or confusion
Instructors can help students overcome these behaviors through coaching techniques

For instructors, coaching is:
Process of giving motivational correction, positive reinforcement, and constructive feedback to students to maintain and improve their performance

slides.title: Coaching
content: Coaching

To be effective, feedback needs to be positive, immediate, direct, and frequent

It can either be as simple as telling the student how well a task has been completed or involve a formal counseling session when a change in negative or inappropriate behavior is required

slides.title: Coaching: Formal Coaching Model Steps
content: Coaching: Formal Coaching Model Steps

slides.title: Coaching
content: Coaching

Feedback from instructors must be objective and precise in its description of desirable and undesirable behavior

Instructors must not fall into the trap of just providing critical phrases, even if they are intended to motivate a student to try again; that type of feedback does not inform the students of their error or explain how to correct it

Good feedback hints at the right answer

slides.title: Coaching
content: Coaching

Asking students questions allows them to stop, think, and recall the information they are attempting to apply

Some students will take longer than others to perform this process, but they will all remember better because they had to recall it themselves

On occasions when students do not recall the information, the instructor can carefully review it with them

slides.title: Motivating and Encouraging Students: Self-Motivation Influences
content: Motivating and Encouraging Students: Self-Motivation Influences

slides.title: Motivating and Encouraging Students
content: Motivating and Encouraging Students

Fear of failure is a psychological barrier that may prevent people from taking risks

If students believe that an instructor genuinely wants them to succeed and will give them the tools to do so, they are more likely to overcome a fear of failure

slides.title: Motivating and Encouraging Students: Instructional Enhancements
content: Motivating and Encouraging Students: Instructional Enhancements

Provide quality instruction that helps students who try to learn

Provide evidence that student efforts make a difference

Establish clear expectations

Provide continuous feedback about student progress

slides.title: Providing Peer Assistance
content: Providing Peer Assistance

Peer assistance involves having students help each other in the learning process

Students who have grasped a knowledge or skill and can explain it to others make good peer assistants; it helps if they have background experiences that enable them to explain how classroom activities can be applied on the job

slides.title: Mentoring
content: Mentoring

In contrast to a peer assistance arrangement, mentoring situations occur outside the classroom, usually in the job environment

Many instructors have acted as mentors

Instructors often guide the actions of new employees, just as they guide the actions of new students in the learning environment or training evolution

slides.title: Mentoring
content: Mentoring

Instructors, or the organization, may assign a mentor when they know someone who can guide student actions in real experiences on the job

Mentors must be selected for their work experience, subject matter interest, patience, good opinion of the organization, and communication abilities

Primary purpose of mentoring is to prepare students for advancement within the organization with the direction of a positive role model

slides.title: Mentoring: Assisting Students
content: Mentoring: Assisting Students

slides.title: Mentoring: The Concept
content: Mentoring: The Concept

Begins with the direct supervisor

Immediate supervisor or instructor is customarily designated as primary mentor for each student

Military versus nonmilitary functions have different mentoring factors including time and parameters for each role

slides.title: Learning Objective 4
content: Learning Objective 4
Explain strategies used by 	instructors in dealing with classroom 	behavior issues.

slides.title: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues
content: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues

When it is necessary to regain the attention of disruptive students who are talking among themselves off topic, instructors may call on one of the individuals

 While trying to not embarrass the person, the instructor summarizes the topic and asks a simple opinion question that directs attention back to the lesson

Doing this more than once is not advised

slides.title: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues
content: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues

Some students feel that they already have superior knowledge to instructors and do not need to be in class

These students may attempt to goad the instructor into revealing inadequacy or ignorance of their subject matter

Such students may also desire to display their knowledge to their peers

slides.title: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues
content: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues

Show confidence in your role as content expert

If you do not know the answer to a question, admit it, and bring the answer back to the class when you can

Respond to the student, but continue to manage class time, and consider the interests of others when engaged in a dialogue with an individual

slides.title: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues
content: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues

Always smile

Do not embarrass students when they expose their limitations

Avoid getting into a battle of wills with students

Let participants know that their questions have merit

slides.title: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues
content: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues

When a student asks a challenging question, chances are that other students have the same one and are too shy or embarrassed to ask

Instructor can redirect the question into an open discussion to get a wider perspective on the topic

 Because of the positive reinforcement, everyone gets involved, all benefit from the discussion, and everyone grows comfortable participating

slides.title: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues
content: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues

A disruptive student may be seeking attention, but instructors must be careful not to reward this behavior by paying too much attention to the actions

Some behaviors will simply stop; some will not

When it does not, the L-E-A-S-T method of progressive disciplinary action is suggested

slides.title: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues: The L-E-A-S-T Method
content: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues: The L-E-A-S-T Method

slides.title: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues
content: Strategies for Dealing with Classroom Issues

An advantage of being in a paramilitary organization such as the law enforcement, fire, and emergency services is that the instructor generally has the authority of an officer in the classroom

Instructors should be prepared to use this authority in order to maintain classroom control, but also plan redirects to avoid those circumstances

slides.title: Nondisruptive, Nonparticipating Students
content: Nondisruptive, Nonparticipating Students

May appear to be daydreaming, distracted, or uninterested

In courses where students attend instruction for long periods of time, instructors may use several methods to engage them

Instructors should ask students casually about their attitudes toward the class, or any distractions they may have

slides.title: Nondisruptive, Nonparticipating Students
content: Nondisruptive, Nonparticipating Students

Simple comfort questions during breaks may encourage students to readily provide answers because they appreciate the interest and attention

Depending on the circumstance, the instructor may remind students that they have a responsibility to participate

These students will normally make every attempt to fulfill the class requirements and please an instructor who shows interest in them

slides.title: Shy or Timid Students
content: Shy or Timid Students

May be hesitant or at a loss for words when expected to respond or participate

Instructors should avoid calling on these students until they have become comfortable with the class and instructor

Instructors should encourage shy students to participate in informal or small-group discussions

slides.title: Shy or Timid Students: Becoming Comfortable
content: Shy or Timid Students: Becoming Comfortable

slides.title: Bored or Uninterested Students
content: Bored or Uninterested Students

Many quiet students may be above average in ability, but they may drift mentally due to many circumstances, including a perceived lack of opportunity to interrupt a lecture for a question

Instructors can redirect attention by asking direct questions or beginning activities that require student participation

slides.title: Bored or Uninterested Students: Signs of Daydreaming and Boredom
content: Bored or Uninterested Students: Signs of Daydreaming and Boredom

slides.title: Bored or Uninterested Students
content: Bored or Uninterested Students

Students who are uninterested often display little energy and attention

When this behavior continues through multiple types of instructor interventions
Instructors may check with their supervisors or other instructors to determine whether the students have exhibited personal or other problems

Instructors will want to gather as much information as possible to plan strategies for working with these students

slides.title: Bored or Uninterested Students: Student Experiences
content: Bored or Uninterested Students: Student Experiences

slides.title: Disruptive, Nonparticipating Students
content: Disruptive, Nonparticipating Students

Act in a way that is noticeably inappropriate for a learning environment 

May distract the class by being overly talkative, showing a lack of respect for the instructor or the course, or trying simply to draw attention to themselves

In addition to stalling class progress, this behavior may create a safety hazard

slides.title: Disruptive, Nonparticipating Students
content: Disruptive, Nonparticipating Students

Instructors should not allow these students to control the class and should attempt to redirect students’ energy toward constructive participation

If attempts to change the students’ behavior fail, instructors should take another action, such as asking them to leave the session and clearly informing them that cooperation and constructive participation is expected upon their return

Continually disruptive students may be reported

slides.title: Talkative Students
content: Talkative Students

Talkative students may monopolize discussions and prevent others from participating without intending harm

Instructors must recapture attention of groups that may sit together, entertain each other during discussion 

Strategies include private appeals to one or more students in the disruptive group or making pointed recommendations to the group to continue their discussions outside of class time

slides.title: Attention-Seeking Students
content: Attention-Seeking Students

May use group situations to perform and gain attention for themselves

May need coaching to know when to stop and share the focus

Instructor should encourage other students to respond, reminding the student that other classmates need an opportunity to answer

slides.title: Attention-Seeking Students
content: Attention-Seeking Students

When the attention-seeking student does not demonstrate willingness to work with an instructor’s redirects, the instructor may offer an ultimatum

When students understand safe behaviors and cooperation are important, expected, and enforced, instructors will have few if any problems

When problems arise, instructors should always follow the organization’s disciplinary policies and procedures

slides.title: Attention-Seeking Students
content: Attention-Seeking Students

Instructors should never tolerate inappropriate behavior that creates unsafe conditions for students

Examples of safety violations related to an attention-seeking student’s behavior may serve as a strong object lesson for the entire class

Instructors must be careful not to use these examples as a reprimand to the disruptive student, but as a teaching opportunity for the class

slides.title: Reasons for Disruptive Behavior: Instructor-Caused Disruptive Behavior
content: Reasons for Disruptive Behavior: Instructor-Caused Disruptive Behavior

Some disruptive behavior results from the actions of the instructor

Instructor must demonstrate that he or she is a master of the information presented in the classroom, but this authority must never be used to intimidate a student in any way

Instructor should practice demonstrating respect and patience

slides.title: Reasons for Disruptive Behavior: Instructor-Caused Disruptive Behavior
content: Reasons for Disruptive Behavior: Instructor-Caused Disruptive Behavior

Overseeing some types of learning environments, particularly skills training, can be frustrating to an instructor who wants to help students succeed

Instructors should not rely on strict rules that may become barriers to learning

Instructors should prepare to adjust to the needs of students, the changing environment, and the subject matter

slides.title: Reasons for Disruptive Behavior: Instructor-Caused Disruptive Behavior
content: Reasons for Disruptive Behavior: Instructor-Caused Disruptive Behavior

Students can often easily recognize an unprepared instructor

Instructor preparation and practice increase the ability for all participants to enjoy learning

Instructors must maintain awareness and control of the timing of the class

content: Reasons for Disruptive Behavior: Student-Caused Disruptive Behavior

content: Reasons for Disruptive Behavior: Student-Caused Disruptive Behavior

content: Causes of Disruptive Behavior

content: Student Disruptive Behavior: Possible Reasons

slides.title: Student Disruptive Behavior
content: Student Disruptive Behavior

May understand need for class but are uninterested in the subject matter

May need more direction in matching needs with instructor teaching style

May need help to determine relationship between needs and course content for themselves

May need to feel their opinion is valued

slides.title: Learning Objective 5
content: Learning Objective 5
Describe ways instructors can take formal disciplinary action.

slides.title: Taking Formal Disciplinary Action
content: Taking Formal Disciplinary Action

When an instructor is unable to help a student accept or settle into a routine, disciplinary action becomes necessary

Instructors should be familiar with organizational policies and follow them closely

Student’s behavior should be thoroughly documented in order to justify disciplinary actions

slides.title: Taking Formal Disciplinary Action: Collecting Data
content: Taking Formal Disciplinary Action: Collecting Data

Record date and behavior whenever class must be interrupted to manage specific student’s behavior

Keep documentation in secure location

Draft memo to student, detailing disruptive behavior

Send copy of memo to chief/manager and training officer

Await formal action by training division

slides.title: Taking Formal Disciplinary Action
content: Taking Formal Disciplinary Action

Training organization regulations may provide instructors with the option of dismissing an individual from a class

If so, a paper trail of notes, memos, and counseling forms is essential to prove that the action was taken with justification

Documentation must show progressive reprimands or disciplinary actions that may end with or result in an individual being removed from a class

slides.title: Learning Objective 1
content: Learning Objective 1
Discuss agencies and organizations where instructors can find the most current information about safety guidelines and regulations.

slides.title: Federal Government Agencies
content: Federal Government Agencies

In North America, are responsible for developing, regulating, and ensuring safe workplace policies
National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety (CCOHS)
National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

slides.title: Federal Government Agencies
content: Federal Government Agencies
Other organizations may have more specialized regulatory information that instructors may need to seek out for specific training situations

slides.title: Resources: Safety Guidelines, Regulations, and Information
content: Resources: Safety Guidelines, Regulations, and Information

Department of Homeland Security (DHS)

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)

Department of Transportation (DOT)

Department of Defense (DoD)

slides.title: NOTE
content: NOTE
Agencies in both Canada and the U.S. share information and materials. Some Canadian safety regulations are based on or modeled after NFPA standards and OSHA regulations.

slides.title: State/Provincial and Local Safety and Health Agencies
content: State/Provincial and Local Safety and Health Agencies

States/provinces and local governmental occupational safety and health agencies often include review and enforcement functions

In Canada and the U.S., states/provinces or local agencies may have to follow regulations that differ from, expand upon, or exceed national rules

May also have to follow additional regulations not addressed at federal level, such as those mandated by state/provincial environmental agencies

slides.title: State/Provincial and Local Safety and Health Agencies
content: State/Provincial and Local Safety and Health Agencies

Instructors should know federal, state/provincial, local regulations are likely to impact training evolutions or how to contact appropriate agencies regarding applicable regulations, but not limit inquiries to fire and emergency services regulations

State/provincial and local agencies may also have safety regulations written for other industries or organizations that apply to fire and emergency services training

slides.title: State/Provincial and Local Safety and Health Agencies
content: State/Provincial and Local Safety and Health Agencies

Regulatory agencies may have consultants or educators who can review pertinent safety regulations with instructors who are planning a training curriculum or course

Health departments or agencies can also provide 

Statistical data and safety programs

Information on diseases and their prevention

slides.title: Standards-Writing Organizations
content: Standards-Writing Organizations

Standards-writing organizations develop and issue operating procedures and design requirements for various industries:
Including the fire and emergency services
Arrange for a committee
Composed of industry representatives
Build an overall standard as members develop a consensus on individual topics
These standards do not become law until a government authority adopts them

slides.title: Learning Objective 2
content: Learning Objective 2
Describe the responsibilities of the instructor as a safety role model.

slides.title: Instructor as Safety Role Model
content: Instructor as Safety Role Model

In addition to describing safety guidelines, instructors must demonstrate and reinforce these guidelines equally with students and staff

Following safety guidelines or plans has a significant effect on reducing injuries and fatalities in training and at emergency incidents

Instructors must be empowered to plan, change, and present courses that follow safety requirements

slides.title: CAUTION
content: CAUTION
If a policy is in place and you, as an instructor, do not follow its guidelines, you may be held liable for injuries to students.

slides.title: Instructor as Safety Role Model
content: Instructor as Safety Role Model

Instructors must devote appropriate time to discussing aspects of safety

Safety provisions and briefings should be planned well before the activity starts and reflected during the training session through awareness and practice

slides.title: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents: Actions Before or During Training
content: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents: Actions Before or During Training

Describing applicable safety requirements or procedures to students

Creating a training and safety plan for any high-hazard drill or application, and briefing all instructors and students on the plan before training begins

Planning carefully for training scenarios

slides.title: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents: Actions Before or During Training
content: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents: Actions Before or During Training

Ensuring that appropriately trained personnel assist in supervising scenarios

Inspecting and repairing tools, equipment, props, and apparatus before starting training sessions

Assigning a safety officer to each training scenario based upon a prepared training and safety plan

slides.title: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents: Actions Before or During Training
content: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents: Actions Before or During Training

Assigning additional personnel (more than the minimum) for safety positions depending upon the scale of the training evolution and the severity of danger

Describing the proper safeguards and equipment used for preventing accidents

Describing possible hazards and explaining the necessary precautions

slides.title: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents: Actions Before or During Training
content: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents: Actions Before or During Training

Safety briefing: 
Students on relevant techniques,
Procedures, 
Tools, 
Facility characteristics
Appropriate safety rules before starting the evolution
Courtesy of U.S. Air Force

slides.title: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents: Actions Before or During Training
content: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents: Actions Before or During Training

Reviewing emergency procedures, emergency evacuation plans, and verbal or alarm alerts with students before the evolution
Modeling and reinforcing safety policies and procedures by personally adhering to them
Watching for behaviors that can contribute to unsafe conditions:
Improper attitude, complacency, or lack of knowledge or skill

slides.title: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents
content: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents

When planning practical training evolutions, instructors must identify and eliminate potential hazards
Instructors must also plan to address the necessary precautions to prevent injury while training
Train students to recognize job hazards
Teach them how to control or eliminate these hazards
These precautions help minimize the level of risk and prevent injuries

slides.title: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents
content: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents

When planning high-hazard training evolutions
Instructor should appoint another qualified individual as the safety officer for the training evolution

The safety officer must be familiar with the logistics involved in the evolution including the purpose and scope of the training, and what may happen at any given time

slides.title: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents
content: Increasing Awareness and Preventing Accidents

Fire and emergency services programs often train nonemergency services employees

Although these students may not be required to perform all aspects of the curriculum on their jobs, instructors must enforce all safety procedures as these employees participate in the course

Regardless whether all training procedures apply to these students, they must still follow safety guidelines

slides.title: NOTE
content: NOTE

Establish and use training and safety plans during all types of emergency incidents and high-hazard training evolutions. 
Use of a personnel accountability system.

slides.title: Learning Objective 3
content: Learning Objective 3
Identify ways that instructors plan for safe training.

slides.title: Verifying Instructor Skill Level
content: Verifying Instructor Skill Level

Instructors should be honest with themselves about their own ability levels and knowledge

An instructor certified to a proficiency level in a skill may find he or she needs to relearn the skill if it has not been actively used; some skills change over time

An instructor having the appropriate certifications but not confident in his or her competence in teaching the skills should gain current skills or recommend a better qualified instructor to teach the course

slides.title: Planning for Safe Training: Verifying Instructor Skill Level
content: Planning for Safe Training: Verifying Instructor Skill Level

An instructor may be capable of teaching skills at the appropriate level, but may not have the appropriate certifications to teach a topic; should work with supervisors to update certifications whenever possible

Training cannot continue without an available instructor who has the appropriate skills and qualifications

Instructors should take advantage of continuing education opportunities that will benefit their ability to offer timely, accurate, and safe training

slides.title: Inspecting and Repairing Facilities and Props
content: Inspecting and Repairing Facilities and Props

Equipment evaluation and inspections ensure that class props and other instructional technology tools are available and in working condition before a class session begins

If equipment is unsafe or damaged, the instructor should report this to the AHJ

Session may be rescheduled, adjusted to exclude the type of equipment, or moved to another location with equipment in functional repair

slides.title: Identifying Training Hazards
content: Identifying Training Hazards

Instructors should be familiar and comfortable with prepared lesson plans, the training facility, any training props, and the skills and hazards involved in the evolution to be conducted

Students should be informed during the training briefing of hazards they will face as part of training

Instructors will need to modify the lesson plan to include appropriate safety instructions

slides.title: Psychomotor Skills Demonstrations
content: Psychomotor Skills Demonstrations

Instructor should guide and coach students as they practice

Have the student critique and coach each other as they practice in small groups

Once or twice during a practice session, instructors may need to demonstrate the entire skill

slides.title: Psychomotor Skills Demonstrations
content: Psychomotor Skills Demonstrations

Instructors must show the skill steps correctly and in sequence; the end of the session is a good time to do this

Students should be encouraged to practice skills during rest breaks, during free time, and at the beginning of the next training session

When students perfect the skill, they are ready for evaluation

slides.title: Psychomotor Skills Demonstrations
content: Psychomotor Skills Demonstrations

Planning, preparation, and practice are essential to a successful skills demonstration

The instructor who does not appear proficient at a skill will lose credibility with students and waste valuable training time by having to repeat or correct skill steps

Explain a simple training evolution.

slides.title: Simple Training Evolutions
content: Simple Training Evolutions

Simple training evolutions share some training techniques in common with psychomotor skills training

The main difference is the number of students involved and the training location

Psychomotor skills training is often conducted in a classroom or lab, with the potential for a large number of students learning at the same time

slides.title: Simple Training Evolutions
content: Simple Training Evolutions

Simple training evolutions involve small numbers of students performing a single skill that requires only a few tasks

Training evolutions typically take place on a fireground or other outdoor learning environment regardless of their size or complexity

Instructor should inspect and be familiar with tools and equipment

Evolutions may involve small groups and require one or two instructors

Students repeat the evolution, rotating positions to experience and practice each part of the skill until they able to perform the evolution without error

Remember to use positive reinforcement when applicable.
